vignette:
Jessica, a twenty-five-year-old bus driver, had been a soldier three years earlier, driving supply trucks through contested terrain. One afternoon a roadside IED detonated under her vehicle. The blast wave threw her against the door frame, and she spent the next forty-five minutes pinned inside as the Humvee burned, watching the smoke billow and listening to the radio crackle with panicked voices she could not answer. The dizziness from the concussion lingered for weeks, and the unpredictability of that moment-the normal road that became a kill zone, the suddenness of the explosion-had rewired something in her. When she returned stateside, she took the bus driver job because it was available and she could sit, but she soon discovered that every shift was a minefield of memory.

A congested intersection made her chest tighten. A passenger swaying into her peripheral vision sent a jolt of adrenaline through her arms. She began scanning her mirrors obsessively, checking each stop for anything out of place, and she had come to believe that she could only feel somewhat at ease if she pressed her back against the driver-side wall of the cab, where no one could approach from behind. The physical reactions-sweating, heart racing, a sick wave of dizziness-arrived without warning, triggered by any hint of unpredictability: a sudden brake, a detour, a rider who stood too close to her seat. These moments convinced her that she was no longer capable of handling even ordinary life. She told herself that the trauma had destroyed her, that nothing felt meaningful anymore because she was just a person waiting for the next surprise to undo her.

The causal loop tightened over months. Each stressful driving situation-a honk from a frustrated motorist, a child running across the street-made her body react, and each reaction reinforced her belief that she was broken, that her life had been hollowed out. That belief, in turn, made her more vigilant: if she was already a wreck, then any small surprise could push her over the edge, so she scanned harder. The constant scanning, meanwhile, made her notice more potential triggers-the wobble of a bicycle, the glint of a soda can that looked out of place-and those observations fed back into her sense that her world had become a series of unpredictable threats. She also noticed that the dizziness, which she had assumed was just a leftover physical symptom, now seemed to flare whenever she felt hopeless and certain that her life would never recover. She would pull over after a dizzy spell, shake her head, and mutter to herself that she could not even drive a bus anymore-and then the thought itself would make her neck muscles tense and her peripheral vision narrow, searching for what might ambush her next.

Her avoidance had become a quiet geography. She took only the same two routes, memorized the potholes and the timing of traffic lights, and she refused any passenger who smelled faintly of diesel fuel, because the odor pulled her straight back into the smoke. She stopped seeing friends because they asked about her plans, and the future felt like an unknown road she could not bear to navigate. What finally brought her to the clinic was a morning when she nearly merged into a car because she had been too busy checking her side-view mirror for something that was not there. She sat in the parking lot afterward, shaking, and she understood that she could not keep driving that bus without help. She was terrified that she would never be capable again, but she was even more afraid of what would happen if she did not try.
